near_miss.lead: Night and inability to sleep: nótt / nǽtr, sofa / svefni beside ἀΰπνους νύκτας.
near_miss.why_not: Homer corpus search confirms the repeated sleepless-night wording at Iliad 9.325 and Odyssey 19.340. Norse has an ordinary finite inability construction, whereas Greek has an adjective modifying nights and a verb of passing the night. The nightmare in bundle 202 is not even sleeplessness. Cognate night and sleep vocabulary describes an obvious circumstance; there is no distinctive shared formula or matching rhetorical structure.

near_miss.lead: This world and the other: í þvísa ljósi ok í ǫðru beside asmin loke.
near_miss.why_not: The Norse oath is explicitly Christian and juxtaposes this life and the next; the supplied Atharvavedic line mentions residence in this world and its surrounding ritual concerns sacrificial authorization. Even if the light/world vocabulary is compared, the second member and oath function are not shared. Not enough to reconstruct inherited wording.

The Latin partner describes actual frozen or wet timber, not hostile advice. Direct search of the Edda text found further cold-counsel wording (OCR lines 5859 and 6774), but these are additional Germanic witnesses and supply no independent branch. Internal traditionality is not evidence here for an inherited Indo-European formula.

near_miss.why_not: The Norse pivot is a genealogical chain, not a coordinated parents merism. Several partners do coordinate parents, while others concern incest, secrecy between generations, or divine parentage. The Irish athar and máthar in G301035 are genitives governed by tig, and the Homeric father/mother pair names actual parents. These natural family combinations lack a distinctive shared poetic or syntactic feature sufficient for an inheritance claim.

near_miss.lead: Weapon brilliance and the sun: Skildir blika; sólin skínn; солнце блестить.
near_miss.why_not: The saga explains how sunlight on shields reveals an ambush. The Russian epic compares a sharpened weapon with the shining sun. Cognate sun vocabulary and the potentially related blika/блестить do not preserve the same relation: a causal observation becomes a simile. The late Russian witness and natural visibility of metal leave independent formation very plausible. A narrow Homer sentence search for sun plus armour terms returned no confirming match; it is not evidence of corpus-wide absence.

near_miss.lead: Loving someone as one’s eyes: ann henni sem augum í hǫfði sér.
near_miss.why_not: The expression occurs in the supplied following context. Neither Greek bundle partner has the eye-comparison. Latin corpus searches found a much closer parallel, recorded separately as a search lead, but no second slab anchor supports that phrase. No anchored claim.

near_miss.lead: A tree does not fall at the first blow: eigi fellr tré við it fyrsta hǫgg.
near_miss.why_not: The recurrence within the saga establishes a proverb. The Iliadic partner concerns Hector dying under a spear, not repeated blows or a tree; the other bundle partners lack the proverb. Latin searches for tree plus blow/fall yielded Catullus 64 and Lucretius 6 passages without the first-blow maxim. No cross-branch phrase is established.

near_miss.lead: Alternating blood-red and grass-pale: sem blóð; fǫlr sem gras.
near_miss.why_not: The Latin partner has the flower of life, not facial pallor. A Latin sentence search for grass with pallor found no match. A search in the available Sappho selection did not recover the recalled grass-colour comparison, and I do not treat a recalled but unlocated passage as a witness. The supplied anchors do not support the figure; no claim.

near_miss.lead: Approaching a superior’s knees in supplication: fara fyrir kné.
near_miss.why_not: The supplied Plautine genu is an instrument of collision in a comic demand to clear the street, not supplication. Homer corpus searches found genuine knee-supplication, recorded as a separate search lead. The additional slab context at Iliad 22.240 has supplication, but not the same motion-before-knees construction; a familiar gesture with only one secure cognate noun does not justify an anchored inherited-phrase claim.

near_miss.lead: A wound near the heart: nǽr hjarta; hṛdayeṣu / hṛdi.
near_miss.why_not: The saga uses a wound close to the heart figuratively for grief over a father’s death. The Atharvavedic partners place intention or a therapeutic power in the heart; they do not share the wound, kinship loss, or syntax. The common body-part word alone is insufficient.

search_lead.cognate: Norse augum (dative plural of auga) and Latin oculis (ablative plural of oculus) continue the Indo-European eye stem *h₃ekʷ-. Love verbs/affection predicates are renewed, not asserted cognates.
search_lead.argument: The following context of the slab anchor compares a husband’s affection for his wife to affection for his own eyes. Latin repeatedly uses one’s eyes as the standard for exceptional affection. This is a closer rhetorical match than the assigned partners, with Norse equality versus Latin superiority. Worth separate review as possible inherited comparison with lexical renewal; bodily-value metaphors and medieval transmission remain alternatives. The Latin wording was located directly in LASLA; it is not a slab anchor.

search_lead.cognate: Norse kné and Greek γούνων / γούνατα continue *ǵónu-; the motion, sitting and grasping verbs are not cognate wording.
search_lead.argument: Norse going before chieftains’ knees denotes demeaning petition for support. The Homer search supplies actual petitioners sitting before or grasping the recipient’s knees. The shared anatomical focus and supplication context merit separate review, but the Norse phrase need not encode literal grasping, and a widely available ritual gesture is insufficient by itself to prove a PIE formula. The assigned Latin partner lacks this function.

error.correct_reading: Eyvindr (personal name), genitive singular; suppress the mapping to *h₂ew.
error.evidence: It is the named father in dóttir Eyvindar, followed by his byname karfa. The form is a proper name, not a free lexical item meaning away/off.

error.correct_reading: gegna, preterite subjunctive singular, here suit/turn out for; remove the yawn-root equation rather than substituting an uncertain PIE root.
error.evidence: The construction oss gegndi verst concerns what would turn out worst for the speakers. Norse gegna is not gína, the verb to gape/yawn; the supplied *ǵʰeh₂- mapping confuses unrelated words.

error.correct_reading: Exclude the modern editorial note from epic-text comparison units.
error.evidence: The context heading is Notes, and the unit discusses the historical events underlying the song, including the uprising at Tver and the identification of the Tatar official through Russian chronicles. This is modern commentary on a song, not its wording.
